title: AI Engineer — Level 3: Production Systems
description: Advanced RAG, fine-tuning decisions, eval design, agent architectures, and serving fundamentals expected of a senior engineer.

questions.prompt: Design the retrieval stage for a RAG system over 2M heterogeneous enterprise documents. Cover hybrid search, re-ranking, and metadata — and justify each component.
questions.answer_notes: Hybrid retrieval: BM25/keyword catches exact terms (IDs, error codes, names) that embeddings blur; dense vectors catch paraphrase and semantics; fuse with RRF. First-stage retrieval casts a wide net (top 50-100), then a cross-encoder re-ranker scores query-document pairs jointly for precision in the final top 5-10 — bi-encoders can't model token-level interaction, cross-encoders can but are too slow for the full corpus, hence the two-stage design. Metadata filtering (department, date, ACL) narrows the candidate space and enforces permissions before ranking. Close with evaluation: labeled query set, recall@k per stage, and monitoring drift as documents change.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Full retrieval-architecture design with justification, standard senior-level system question.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder demands 'fine-tune a model on our data' to fix quality problems. How do you evaluate whether fine-tuning is actually the right tool, and what alternatives do you rule in or out first?
questions.answer_notes: First diagnose the failure: knowledge gaps → RAG (fine-tuning is poor at injecting facts and goes stale); format/style/tone inconsistency → few-shot prompts, then SFT if scale justifies it; capability gaps on hard reasoning → better base model. Fine-tuning wins when: stable, high-volume, narrow task; latency/cost pressure to move to a smaller model; behavior (style, schema adherence) rather than knowledge. Costs people forget: labeled data pipeline, eval harness before/after, re-tuning on every base-model upgrade, hosting/serving the custom model. The senior answer is a decision framework plus 'measure with an eval set first', not a yes/no.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Tests judgment and stakeholder pushback, not just technique.

questions.prompt: You use an LLM-as-judge to score your chatbot's answers. Which is the most serious methodological risk?
options: The judge has systematic biases (position, verbosity, self-preference) that don't cancel out, so scores drift from human judgment
The judge model costs slightly more per call than embedding-based metrics
LLM judges cannot output numeric scores
questions.answer_notes: Known judge biases: preferring longer answers, preferring the first-listed candidate in pairwise setups, favoring outputs in its own style, and rubric drift. Mitigations: calibrate against a human-labeled subset, randomize positions, use pairwise comparisons with swapped orders, pin judge model versions, and rubric-based scoring with references. An uncalibrated judge quietly optimizes your product toward judge quirks.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Advanced eval methodology, expected of anyone running model comparisons.

questions.prompt: When do you build a multi-step agent versus a fixed pipeline (chain) for an LLM workflow? Give the trade-offs and one concrete example of each.
questions.answer_notes: Fixed pipeline: known, decomposable task with stable steps — e.g. 'summarize ticket → classify → draft reply'. Predictable, testable per-stage, cheap, easy evals. Agent (model chooses actions/tools in a loop): open-ended tasks where the path depends on intermediate findings — e.g. 'debug this failing repo' with Claude Code-style file and shell tools. Costs of agents: compounding error per step, harder evals, unbounded latency/cost, need for guardrails (step limits, permissions, checkpoints). Senior rule of thumb: use the least agency that solves the task; start as a pipeline, add agency only where the branching genuinely lives.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Architecture judgment currently asked in most senior AI-engineer interviews.

questions.prompt: What does the KV cache in transformer inference store, and what problem does it solve?
options: Keys and values of already-processed tokens per layer, so each new token only computes attention against cached states instead of re-encoding the whole sequence
The most frequent user queries and their final answers
Model weights quantized to int8 for memory savings
Gradients from the last fine-tuning run
questions.answer_notes: Autoregressive generation would otherwise recompute K/V for the entire prefix at every step (quadratic total work). Caching K/V per layer makes each decode step linear in sequence length. Consequences: KV cache dominates GPU memory for long contexts (hence paged attention, GQA/MQA, quantized caches), and prompt caching across requests exploits shared prefixes. This is the gateway question to serving-infrastructure depth.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Core serving internals; separates infra-aware engineers from API users.

questions.prompt: You're launching an LLM feature with no existing eval data. Describe how you bootstrap an evaluation suite in the first two weeks and evolve it after launch.
questions.answer_notes: Week 1: write 20-50 golden examples by hand from product specs and edge cases (adversarial inputs, ambiguity, refusal cases); define a rubric per axis (correctness, groundedness, format, safety); wire a harness that runs on every prompt/model change (CI). Week 2: expand with synthetic variations (LLM-generated paraphrases, reviewed by humans) and pilot-user transcripts. Post-launch: mine production logs for failures (thumbs-down, retries, escalations), triage weekly into new eval cases — the eval suite becomes a regression test that only grows. Key senior point: evals before optimization; anything unmeasured will silently regress.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Process-design question showing how the candidate actually ships quality.

questions.prompt: Why does LoRA fine-tuning drastically reduce trainable parameters while preserving quality on most adaptation tasks?
options: Weight updates during adaptation have low intrinsic rank, so learning small low-rank matrices A·B alongside frozen weights captures most of the needed change
It deletes transformer layers that are unused for the target task
It trains only the tokenizer vocabulary
It quantizes the gradients to 4 bits
questions.answer_notes: LoRA freezes W and learns ΔW = A·B with rank r ≪ d, cutting trainable parameters by ~1000x, enabling adapter swapping and cheap multi-tenant serving. The empirical premise: task adaptation lives in a low-rank subspace. QLoRA combines this with a 4-bit quantized frozen base to fine-tune large models on a single GPU. Know r, alpha, and which modules (attention projections) adapters usually target.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Standard PEFT depth-check in senior interviews.

questions.prompt: Your LLM API bill is $80k/month and growing. Walk through a systematic cost-reduction plan that doesn't tank quality.
questions.answer_notes: 1) Measure: cost per feature/request, token breakdown (input vs output), and traffic distribution — usually a few endpoints dominate. 2) Prompt diet: trim boilerplate, deduplicate context, cap retrieval chunks; enable prompt caching for static prefixes (system prompts, tool definitions). 3) Model routing: classify request difficulty, send easy/high-volume traffic to smaller models (e.g. Haiku-class), keep frontier models for hard paths; validate per-tier with evals. 4) Response caching for repeated/canonicalizable queries. 5) Batch and async where latency allows (batch APIs are ~50% cheaper). 6) Consider fine-tuning a small model for the one dominant narrow task. Guardrail: every change ships behind the eval suite; report cost per request alongside quality metrics.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Business-aware engineering; increasingly a make-or-break senior question.

questions.prompt: How do you give a long-running agent 'memory' beyond its context window? Compare at least three mechanisms and their failure modes.
questions.answer_notes: 1) Conversation summarization/compaction: periodically compress history into a summary — cheap, but lossy; critical details can vanish. 2) External memory store (vector or structured): agent writes facts/decisions, retrieves them by relevance — scalable, but retrieval misses and stale/contradictory memories corrupt behavior; needs write discipline and TTLs. 3) Structured scratchpads/files (like a plan.md or task list the agent re-reads): explicit, auditable, works well for agentic coding, but the agent must be prompted to maintain it. 4) Episodic checkpoints for resumability. Design point: separate durable facts (store) from working state (scratchpad) from narrative history (summarize); log memory writes for debuggability.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Frontier-practical agent engineering, now common in senior interviews.
